newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto rejects notion of seeking asylum in Britain.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto rejects notion of seeking asylum in Britain.

text.p: Ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto on Monday rejected any notion she might agree to leave Pakistan to escape possible prosecution for corruption.
"The question does not arise of my seeking asylum in Britain or anywhere else," she told Reuters at her farmhouse in Naudero, near her home town of Larkana, as Pakistan's elections began.
"Pakistan is my home and I am going to live in my home," said Bhutto, who was sacked by President Farooq Leghari on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
Bhutto denies the charges. The Supreme Court ruled last week that there was enough evidence to justify Leghari's action and threw out the 43-year-old politician's plea for reinstatement.

"My father also lived here. He could have gone abroad. He chose to die here," said a defiant Bhutto, recalling the fate of her father, former prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who was toppled by the military in 1977 and executed two years later.

She was responding to a report in London's Sunday Times, which quoted senior Pakistani government sources as saying that to avoid a sensitive trial, possible corruption charges against Bhutto and her jailed husband Asif Ali Zardari could be dropped if she agreed to leave the country and abandon politics.
Zardari has been under detention since Bhutto's government was removed on November 5 and faces a charge of conspiring in the September 20 murder of Benazir's estranged brother Murtaza.

After her father's death, Bhutto lived in self-imposed exile in Britain for several years, returning to Pakistan on April 10, 1986 to launch a struggle against former military ruler General Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq, who died in a plane crash in 1988.
The charismatic Bhutto won 1988 elections, but was sacked in 1990 by then president Ghulam Ishaq Khan. She regained power in October 1993, only to be fired a second time by Leghari.
She said the Sunday Times report appeared to be part of an disinformation campaign organised by her political rivals.

"Now my opponents are getting desperate that their tactics have not worked, so they are now trying to feed such stories," she said. "It is very interesting to note how many stories have come in the foreign press on the eve of this election to try and influence it. Such tactics are not going to work.
"There is no truth in these stories at all and the people of Pakistan know me and I know them well," Bhutto declared.

"During the very worst time I stayed here and I continue to stay here. The fact is my opponents are scared of me because they can't defeat me politically so they are always resorting to dirty tricks. The dirty tricks are not going to work."
Hundreds of people waving flags of Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) and making victory signs turned out to greet her when she flew to Larkana in Sindh province from Karachi on Sunday.
"Prime minister Benazir Bhutto," they chanted. "Benazir, you will be remembered as long as the sun and moon are there."
"Our party position is very strong and we hope to win the elections if they are not rigged," Bhutto said later, her voice hoarse from a hectic period of campaigning across Pakistan.
"I have told my party leaders to keep a strict watch on rigging by our opponents," she said as she sat at home, sprinkling salt on a guava grown in one of her orchards.
